definition: Spurious means false but made to seem genuine or plausible.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word spurious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know spurious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The signed jersey proved spurious: the 'autograph' had been applied by machine, ink, smudge, and all.
A questionable claim merely invites doubt—it may yet check out; a spurious one is actually false, dressed up to look sound.
Fraudulent moves past spurious into crime: a spurious quote may fool people innocently, while a fraudulent document is deployed to cheat someone out of something.

Counterfeit is for physical fakes manufactured to pass as the real article — bills, designer bags, forged papers you can hold. Spurious lives one level up, in claims and content: a quotation or a result that is false but dressed to look sound. If the fake is an object, counterfeit is the sharper word.

Bogus is the casual, hallway word for fake — a bogus excuse, a bogus phone number — and it passes no judgment on craftsmanship. Spurious is its formal cousin and adds a charge: the falsehood was dressed up to survive inspection. A bogus claim may fool no one; a spurious one is built to.

Phony is informal and aims mostly at people and their manners — a phony smile, a phony accent. Spurious rarely describes a person at all: it targets claims, credentials, and evidence that are false but made to seem genuine. Call the salesman phony and his miracle testimonials spurious.

Latin spurius survives in English only inside spurious itself—no cousins, no everyday relatives. Anchor it to its story instead: a word for uncertain parentage that came to describe any claim or thing whose 'parents'—its sources and origins—are not what they are said to be.
Spurious means false but made to seem genuine or plausible.
The county fair's 'moon rock' drew crowds until a geologist borrowed it for a weekend.
Her report ran three sentences: the specimen was spurious—quarry basalt, tumbled smooth—and its certificate of authenticity had been issued by an agency that does not exist.
Spurious does a job that 'fake' does only loosely: it stresses that the falseness is dressed to pass inspection.
A toy banana is fake; a lab result invented to look like real data is spurious.
Spurious is the scholar's word for fakes built to pass: spurious quotations, statistics, pedigrees.

Keep it apart from its unit-mates on the truth-and-falsehood shelf: fallacious condemns reasoning, distortion names real facts twisted out of shape, and veracity is the truthfulness all of them offend against.

For decades, wellness articles repeated the claim that humans use only ten percent of their brains, often attributing it to the psychologist William James.
For her science-fair project, Priya Raman decided to trace the claim to its source.
The trail was impressive on its surface: each article cited an earlier one, and the oldest cited 'a Harvard study, 1936.' But the study did not exist.
The archive had no such paper, and James had written no such sentence; the citation was spurious, invented once and copied ever since.
Priya's poster ended with the chain of borrowed footnotes and a single question: had anyone, in ninety years, ever looked?
